name: Label Spreading
analogy: Think of it as the same crowded trading floor, but the name tags on the well-known traders are written in pencil. Neighbors still copy the tags around them, yet a known trader whose neighbors all disagree can be talked out of their own tag, a little.

steps.title: Describe every bar as a row of numbers
steps.description: Each bar, labelled or not, becomes a row of scaled features such as recent return, volume against average and distance from a moving average. Scaling keeps any one feature from dominating the similarity between bars.
steps.inExample: 1,500 five-minute MNQ bars are each described by 6 scaled features. 90 of them have a known outcome.

steps.title: Link look-alike bars and balance the links
steps.description: Each bar is connected to its most similar bars, and the link strengths are then balanced so that bars in a crowded area do not shout over bars in a sparse area. This balancing is what separates it from Label Propagation.
steps.inExample: Each bar gets 10 links. After balancing, a bar in a crowded cluster and a bar in a quiet corner carry comparable weight.

steps.title: Give the known bars a starting vote
steps.description: Bars with a known outcome start with a firm vote for up or for down. Bars without an outcome start with no vote. Unlike Label Propagation, these starting votes are remembered but not locked.
steps.inExample: The 90 known bars start with votes, 47 for up and 43 for down. The other 1,410 start with none.

steps.title: Let every bar mix its own vote with its neighbors
steps.description: In each round, a bar's new opinion is mostly what its neighbors currently say, plus a smaller share of its own starting vote. A single dial sets how large that own share is; a larger dial keeps the known labels more stubborn.
steps.inExample: The dial keeps 20 percent of each bar's own starting vote and takes 80 percent from neighbors.

steps.title: Repeat until the opinions stop moving
steps.description: The mixing is repeated until the opinions settle. Because the pull back toward the starting vote never disappears, the result is a compromise between what a bar was told and what its surroundings say.
steps.inExample: After about 30 rounds the opinions stop changing.

steps.title: Read the final shares, including for known bars
steps.description: Every bar ends with a share of up and a share of down. A known bar whose neighborhood strongly disagrees can end on the other side, which flags a label worth rechecking.
steps.inExample: The 11:40 bar was labelled up, but 7 of its 10 neighbors lean down, so it ends at 46 percent up and flips to down.

useFor.task: Labelling bars when the known labels may be noisy
useFor.example: Spreading outcome labels on MNQ 5-minute bars where a few labels came from a rough rule and some are probably wrong.
Listing the labelled bars whose final share points the other way, so a person can look at those bars on the chart.

useFor.task: Growing a training set for a later model
useFor.example: Turning 90 reliable labels into a few thousand labelled bars before training a tree ensemble on the walk-forward folds.

useFor.task: Regime tagging from a few examples
useFor.example: Marking some stretches as trending or ranging and letting similar stretches inherit the tag.

avoidWhen: You must score each new bar the instant it closes; the web has to be rebuilt to include it, so a model that learns a reusable rule is a better fit.
Your known labels are exact, such as outcomes already measured; then the pencil-tag softness only throws away good information and Label Propagation is the cleaner choice.

example.scenario: A researcher has 1,500 five-minute MNQ bars, 90 with a known outcome: whether the close 6 bars (30 minutes) later was above or below that bar's close. One known bar at 11:40 looks suspicious, and the researcher wants to know whether its surroundings agree with its label.

input.summary: A table of 1,500 bars described by 6 scaled features, with labels on only 90 of them.

fields.name: bars in the web
fields.meaning: All five-minute bars in the sample, labelled and unlabelled together.

fields.name: bars with a known outcome
fields.meaning: Bars whose close 6 bars later is already known and given as a starting vote.

fields.name: links per bar
fields.meaning: How many look-alike bars each bar is connected to.

fields.name: share of a bar's own vote kept
fields.meaning: How strongly a bar holds to its starting label instead of its neighbors' opinion.

fields.name: original label of the 11:40 bar
fields.meaning: The label the 11:40 bar was given before spreading.

fields.name: close of the 11:40 bar
fields.meaning: The price at which the bar being checked closed.

fields.name: neighbors that lean down
fields.meaning: How many of the bar's ten look-alikes lean toward closed lower.

output.summary: A final share of up and down for the 11:40 bar, and whether its label changed.

fields.name: final share leaning up
fields.meaning: The settled share of the bar's neighborhood and its own vote that points to closed higher.

fields.name: final label
fields.meaning: The side with the larger share after spreading.

fields.name: disagrees with original label
fields.meaning: The final label differs from the label the bar started with, so the label deserves a second look.

example.reading: A flip is a flag, not a correction. Open the 11:40 bar on the chart and check how its outcome was labelled; if many known bars flip in one area, the labelling rule itself may be the problem.
